claim: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease observed with aging that represents the most common form of dementia.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease observed with aging that represents the most common form of dementia.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about Alzheimer's disease.

claim: Therapies targeting end-stage disease plaques, tangles, or inflammation have limited efficacy in Alzheimer's disease.
source: To date, therapies targeting end-stage disease plaques, tangles, or inflammation have limited efficacy.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to clinical trial outcomes and therapeutic approaches discussed in the introduction.

claim: Cell intrinsic neural precursor cell (NPC) dysfunction precedes widespread inflammation and amyloid plaque pathology in a mouse model of AD and human fetal cells harboring mutant amyloid precursor protein.
source: Utilizing a mouse model of AD and human fetal cells harboring mutant amyloid precursor protein, we show cell intrinsic neural precursor cell (NPC) dysfunction precedes widespread inflammation and amyloid plaque pathology, making it the earliest defect in the evolution of the disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study including neurosphere assays, immunofluorescence, and Luminex assays at different time points.

claim: Reversing impaired NPC self-renewal via genetic reduction of USP16 can prevent downstream cognitive defects and decrease astrogliosis in vivo.
source: We demonstrate that reversing impaired NPC self-renewal via genetic reduction of USP16, a histone modifier and critical physiological antagonist of the Polycomb Repressor Complex 1, can prevent downstream cognitive defects and decrease astrogliosis in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests (NOR, Barnes Maze) and GFAP staining in Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice.

claim: Reduction of USP16 led to decreased expression of senescence gene Cdkn2a.
source: Reduction of USP16 led to decreased expression of senescence gene Cdkn2a and mitigated aberrant regulation of the Bone Morphogenetic Signaling (BMP) pathway, a previously unknown function of USP16.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data showing Cdkn2a expression levels in different genotypes.

claim: Reduction of USP16 mitigated aberrant regulation of the Bone Morphogenetic Signaling (BMP) pathway.
source: Reduction of USP16 led to decreased expression of senescence gene Cdkn2a and mitigated aberrant regulation of the Bone Morphogenetic Signaling (BMP) pathway, a previously unknown function of USP16.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data showing enrichment of BMP pathway genes in Tg-SwDI mice and rescue in Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice.

claim: Regulation of the BMP pathway is a previously unknown function of USP16.
source: Reduction of USP16 led to decreased expression of senescence gene Cdkn2a and mitigated aberrant regulation of the Bone Morphogenetic Signaling (BMP) pathway, a previously unknown function of USP16.
evidence: This is a novel finding from the study based on RNA-seq analysis.

claim: USP16 can rescue memory and learning through its regulation of both Cdkn2a and BMP signaling in an AD model.
source: Thus, we reveal USP16 as a novel target in an AD model that can both ameliorate the NPC defect and rescue memory and learning through its regulation of both Cdkn2a and BMP signaling.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral testing data and molecular analyses showing effects on both pathways.

claim: Alzheimer's disease occurs in 10% of individuals over the age of 65.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia, occurring in 10% of individuals over the age of 65 and affecting an estimated 5.5 million people in the United States (Hebert et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hebert et al., 2013.

claim: Alzheimer's disease affects an estimated 5.5 million people in the United States.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia, occurring in 10% of individuals over the age of 65 and affecting an estimated 5.5 million people in the United States (Hebert et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hebert et al., 2013.

claim: There is currently no treatment to stop, prevent, or reverse Alzheimer's disease.
source: Currently, there is no treatment to stop, prevent, or reverse AD, and recent advances with monoclonal antibody therapy targeting plaques, although controversial, might at best only slow progression (Huang and Mucke, 2012; Selkoe, 2019; Sevigny et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple sources discussing therapeutic approaches.

claim: Recent advances with monoclonal antibody therapy targeting plaques might at best only slow progression of Alzheimer's disease.
source: Currently, there is no treatment to stop, prevent, or reverse AD, and recent advances with monoclonal antibody therapy targeting plaques, although controversial, might at best only slow progression (Huang and Mucke, 2012; Selkoe, 2019; Sevigny et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang and Mucke, 2012; Selkoe, 2019; Sevigny et al., 2016.

claim: Alzheimer's disease is characterized clinically by dementia and pathologically by amyloid senile plaques and neurofibrillary tangles.
source: Historically, AD has been understood by its end-stage disease phenotype, characterized clinically by dementia and pathologically by amyloid senile plaques and neurofibrillary tangles (Castellani et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Castellani et al., 2010 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Traditional AD pathologies are thought to begin with amyloid plaque deposition that is associated with inflammation, increased reactive oxygen species (ROS), and neurodegeneration during aging.
source: These traditional AD pathologies are thought to begin with amyloid plaque deposition that is associated with inflammation, increased reactive oxygen species (ROS), and neurodegeneration during aging (Akiyama et al., 2000; Glass et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Akiyama et al., 2000; Glass et al., 2010.

claim: Treatments to decrease formation of plaques have shown only minimal or no improvement in disease progression or outcomes.
source: however, thus far, treatments to decrease formation of plaques have shown only minimal or no improvement in disease progression or outcomes (Knopman et al., 2021; Selkoe, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Knopman et al., 2021; Selkoe, 2019.

claim: Adult neurogenesis is thought to be compromised in AD, contributing to early dementia.
source: Adult neurogenesis is thought to be compromised in AD, contributing to early dementia (Alipour et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alipour et al., 2019.

claim: The decline of neural stem/precursor cell (NPC) function in the subventricular zone (SVZ) and the hippocampus has been established in both aging and various AD mouse models.
source: The decline of neural stem/precursor cell (NPC) function in the subventricular zone (SVZ) and the hippocampus has been established in both aging (Leeman et al., 2018) and various AD mouse models (Haughey et al., 2002; López-Toledano and Shelanski, 2004; Mu and Gage, 2011; Rodríguez et al., 2009; Rodríguez and Verkhratsky, 2011; Sakamoto et al., 2014; Winner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on aging and AD mouse models.

claim: The NPC defects seen in the Tg-SwDI AD mouse model are initially cell-intrinsic and predate inflammation and widespread plaque deposition.
source: Here, we report that the NPC defects seen in an AD mouse model harboring Swedish, Dutch, and Iowa mutations in the amyloid precursor protein (Tg-SwDI) is initially cell-intrinsic and predates inflammation and widespread plaque deposition, which play a role later in the disease.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study including temporal analyses of inflammation, plaque deposition, and NPC function.

claim: The Tg-SwDI model was chosen because mice develop early plaque deposition and cognitive deficits, and express physiologic levels of transgenic human AβPP at approximately 50% the level of endogenous mouse APP.
source: We chose the Tg-SwDI model with mutations confined to APP because mice develop early plaque deposition and cognitive deficits, and express physiologic levels of transgenic human AβPP at approximately 50% the level of endogenous mouse APP (Davis et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Davis et al., 2004.

claim: In the Tg-SwDI model, mice begin to develop amyloid deposition in brain parenchyma as early as 3 months of age and throughout the forebrain by 12 months.
source: In this model, mice begin to develop amyloid deposition in brain parenchyma as early as 3 months of age and throughout the forebrain by 12 months (Davis et al., 2004; Miao et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Davis et al., 2004; Miao et al., 2005.

claim: The Tg-SwDI model develops significant cerebral amyloid angiopathy, which is thought to be a more sensitive predictor of dementia than parenchymal and amyloid plaques.
source: as well as significant cerebral amyloid angiopathy, which is thought to be a more sensitive predictor of dementia than parenchymal and amyloid plaques (Neuropathology Group. Medical Research Council Cognitive Function and Aging Study, 2001; Thal et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Neuropathology Group study, 2001; Thal et al., 2003.

claim: USP16 counteracts self-renewal regulator BMI1 by deubiquitinating histone H2A on Lysine 119 at the Cdkn2a locus, resulting in increased expression of protein products P16 (Ink4a) and P14 (Arf).
source: USP16 counteracts self-renewal regulator BMI1 by deubiquitinating histone H2A on Lysine 119 at the Cdkn2a locus, resulting in increased expression of protein products P16 (Ink4a) and P14 (Arf) (Adorno et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Adorno et al., 2013.

claim: USP16 activity results in increased senescence with a concomitant decrease in self-renewal.
source: This results in increased senescence with a concomitant decrease in self-renewal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of USP16 and Cdkn2a.

claim: Inhibiting USP16 is a potential novel strategy to rescue Cdkn2a-mediated pathologies in AD induced by both p16Ink4a and p19Arf.
source: Here, we demonstrate that inhibiting USP16 is a potential novel strategy to rescue Cdkn2a-mediated pathologies in AD induced by both p16Ink4a and p19Arf.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing rescue of NPC defects and cognitive function in Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice.

claim: The BMP pathway has been known to play a role in NPC function.
source: The BMP pathway has been known to play a role in NPC function.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: BMPR2 is a type II receptor that heterodimerizes with BMPR1a or BMPR1b, and is responsible for transducing BMP signaling downstream to the SMAD proteins, which translocate to the nucleus and can turn on genes related to cell fate and differentiation.
source: Specifically, BMPR2 is a type II receptor that heterodimerizes with BMPR1a or BMPR1b, and is responsible for transducing BMP signaling downstream to the SMAD proteins, which translocate to the nucleus and can turn on genes related to cell fate and differentiation (Chang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2018 and represents established knowledge of BMP signaling.

claim: Levels of BMP2, 4, 6, and 7 expression have been found to increase in the hippocampus and SVZ with age.
source: Levels of BMP2, 4, 6, and 7 expression have been found to increase in the hippocampus and SVZ with age (Yousef et al., 2015; Apostolopoulou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yousef et al., 2015; Apostolopoulou et al., 2017.

claim: Bmpr2 conditional ablation in Ascl1 expressing neural stem cells (NSCs)/NPCs or treatment with BMP inhibitor Noggin results in activation of NSCs, increased cell proliferation, and a rescue of cognitive deficits to levels comparable to young mice.
source: Furthermore, Bmpr2 conditional ablation in Ascl1 expressing neural stem cells (NSCs)/NPCs or treatment with BMP inhibitor Noggin results in activation of NSCs, increased cell proliferation, and a rescue of cognitive deficits to levels comparable to young mice (Meyers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meyers et al., 2016.

claim: Targeting USP16 in a mouse model of AD rescues two aberrant aging pathways, Cdkn2a and BMP, which can restore self-renewal of NPCs, decrease astrogliosis, and retard cognitive decline.
source: For the first time, we show that targeting USP16 in a mouse model of AD rescues two aberrant aging pathways, Cdkn2a and BMP, which can restore self-renewal of NPCs, decrease astrogliosis, and retard cognitive decline (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript and summarized in Figure 1.

claim: Proliferation of NPCs, marked by EdU, SOX2, and GFAP, was increased threefold in the SVZ of 3-month-old Tg-SwDI mice compared to wild type.
source: At 3 months of age, we found that proliferation of NPCs, marked by 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine (EdU) (Chehrehasa et al., 2009), SOX2, and GFAP, was increased threefold in the SVZ of Tg-SwDI mice (p=0.0153; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Hyperproliferation has been linked to a premature decline in stem cell function associated with aging in many tissues including the blood, pancreas, intestine, and mammary gland.
source: In many tissues including the blood, pancreas, intestine, and mammary gland, hyperproliferation has been linked to a premature decline in stem cell function associated with aging (Essers et al., 2009; Krishnamurthy et al., 2006; Scheeren et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Essers et al., 2009; Krishnamurthy et al., 2006; Scheeren et al., 2014.

claim: 3 and 4-month-old Tg-SwDI mice had significantly less regenerative potential of the SVZ cells than that of healthy age-matched control mice.
source: We discovered that 3 and 4-month-old Tg-SwDI mice had significantly less regenerative potential of the SVZ cells than that of healthy age-matched control mice (neurosphere-initiating cell (NIC) frequencies: 1 in 14.5 versus 1 in 7.5, respectively, p=0.00166, Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by extreme limiting dilution analysis data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Bmi1 is required for self-renewal of stem cells in the peripheral and central nervous systems and is responsible for repressing p16Ink4a expression.
source: As Bmi1 is required for self-renewal of stem cells in the peripheral and central nervous systems and is responsible for repressing p16Ink4a expression, we queried if decreased Bmi1 and/or increased Cdkn2a expression was concurrent with the observed decrease in regenerative potential of NPCs from Tg-SwDI mice (Molofsky et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Molofsky et al., 2005.

claim: No significant differences in inflammatory markers were found between Tg-SwDI and WT mice in the SVZ, hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG), and cortex at 3 and 4 months of age.
source: We looked at the SVZ, hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG), and cortex in 3 and 4-month-old mice, but found no significant differences in inflammatory markers between Tg-SwDI and WT mice in any of these regions (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Luminex assay data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No significant differences in Ptgs2 (COX2) mRNA levels were found between WT and Tg-SwDI in the SVZ, DG, or cortex at 3 and 4 months of age.
source: To explore further, we measured mRNA levels of Ptgs2 (COX2), Tnf, Il6, and Il1b utilizing quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), but found no significant differences between WT and Tg-SwDI in either the SVZ, DG, or cortex for Ptgs2, whereas the remaining markers were undetectable using quantitative RT-PCR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Tnf, Il6, and Il1b were undetectable using quantitative RT-PCR in the SVZ, DG, or cortex at 3 and 4 months of age.
source: To explore further, we measured mRNA levels of Ptgs2 (COX2), Tnf, Il6, and Il1b utilizing quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), but found no significant differences between WT and Tg-SwDI in either the SVZ, DG, or cortex for Ptgs2, whereas the remaining markers were undetectable using quantitative RT-PCR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 3 and 4-month-old Tg-SwDI mice showed no evidence of cognitive impairment when subjected to novel object recognition (NOR) testing after 24 hr.
source: Although Tg-SwDI mice are known to exhibit these features, there was no evidence of cognitive impairment in 3 and 4-month-old mice when subjected to novel object recognition (NOR) training and subsequent testing after 24 hr (Ennaceur and Delacour, 1988; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral testing data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Human fetal neurospheres infected with mutant APP (Swedish and Indiana mutations) showed diminished neurosphere-initiating cell (NIC) frequency compared to cells infected with empty vector or with WT APP.
source: Employing the same limiting dilution assay as before, we found diminished NIC frequency of mutant APP-infected human neurospheres compared to cells infected with the empty vector or with WT APP (1 in 10.44 versus 1 in 3.31 and 1 in 10.44 versus 1 in 5.26, respectively, p=3.7e–06 and p=0.00507; Figure 2F and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by limiting dilution assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The self-renewal defect in mutant APP-expressing cells is cell-intrinsic and can be observed in two different AD models with different mutations.
source: This result suggests that the self-renewal defect is cell-intrinsic and can be observed in two different AD models with different mutations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of similar defects in both mouse and human cell models with different APP mutations.

claim: The NPC hyperproliferation observed in 3 and 4-month-old Tg-SwDI mice was not observed in 1-year-old mice.
source: The NPC hyperproliferation in SVZ observed in 3 and 4-month-old Tg-SwDI mice was not observed in 1-year-old mice, demonstrated by the number of EdU+SOX2+GFAP+ cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The defect in self-renewal observed in 3 and 4-month-old Tg-SwDI mice was exacerbated in 1-year-old Tg-SwDI mice.
source: Still, the defect in self-renewal that was observed in the 3 and 4-month-old Tg-SwDI mice was exacerbated in the 1-year-old Tg-SwDI mice (p=0.00625; Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by limiting dilution assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No significant increases in A1 astrocytic markers were observed in the cortex of 1-year-old Tg-SwDI mice compared to WT.
source: With the aim of evaluating astrogliosis, we performed a qPCR for A1 astrocytic markers in the cortex of 1-year-old mice, but did not observe any significant increases in mRNA expression compared to WT (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cells originating from Tg-SwDI mice formed more GFAP+ cells than those from WT controls following differentiation of neurosphere cultures from the SVZ.
source: However, when we looked at differentiation of neurosphere cultures from the SVZ of Tg-SwDI mice and WT controls and analyzed the number of GFAP-expressing cells following differentiation, we found that cells originating from Tg-SwDI mice formed more GFAP+ cells than those from WT controls.
evidence: This is supported by differentiation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: There is a general lineage increase in astrocytes derived from Tg-SwDI NPCs compared to WT NPCs.
source: This suggested that there was a general lineage increase in astrocytes derived from Tg-SwDI NPCs compared to WT NPCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on the differentiation assay data.

claim: 2-year-old Tg-SwDI mice showed an increase in Cd44, Vim, Serping1, and other markers related to pan- and A1-specific astrogliosis compared to WT mice.
source: When we looked at 2-year-old mice by microarray analyses of SVZ, DG, and cortex, we saw an increase in Cd44, Vim, Serping1, and other markers related to pan- and A1-specific astrogliosis and a concomitant inflammatory signature of Tg-SwDI mice compared to WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A, B, respectively, Reinitz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A, B.

claim: A significant increase in GFAP-expressing cells was observed in the cerebral cortex of 2-year-old Tg-SwDI mice compared to WT.
source: We next looked for additional evidence of astrogliosis and observed a significant increase in GFAP-expressing cells in the cerebral cortex of 2-year-old Tg-SwDI mice compared to WT that was not seen in younger Tg-SwDI mice (p<0.0001; Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Reactive astrogliosis is exacerbated by and strongly correlated with aging and later disease progression in the Tg-SwDI model.
source: This suggests that reactive astrogliosis is exacerbated by and strongly correlated with aging and later disease progression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal pattern of astrogliosis observed in the study.

claim: Expression of Cdkn2a was increased with aging and even more so in the Tg-SwDI cortex.
source: In line with our findings thus far, expression of the well-studied gene, Cdkn2a, known for its increased expression with aging and critical function of inhibiting stem cell self-renewal during development and throughout the lifespan, was increased with aging and even more so in the Tg-SwDI cortex (Figure 3E). (Molofsky et al., 2003; Park et al., 2003; Sun et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E and citations to Molofsky et al., 2003; Park et al., 2003; Sun et al., 2004.

claim: There is a premature reduction of self-renewal capacity of NPCs, but not necessarily a decrease in the total number of neural progenitor cells in the Tg-SwDI model.
source: Taken together with our data showing an increase in EdU+SOX2+GFAP+ cells in Tg-SwDI mice SVZ at an early age, our extreme limiting dilution assay in older mice, and expression changes of Cdkn2a and Bmi1, we infer a premature reduction of self-renewal capacity of NPCs, but not necessarily a decrease in the total number of neural progenitor cells in our Tg-SwDI model.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of experimental data.

claim: A neural stem cell defect and early cognitive decline predate detectable inflammation and reactive astrogliosis in Tg-SwDI mice.
source: These results suggest that a neural stem cell defect and early cognitive decline predate detectable inflammation and reactive astrogliosis in Tg-SwDI mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal sequence of events observed in the study.

claim: There was a complete restoration of the NIC frequency in Tg-SwDI/Cdkn2a-/- cells compared to age-matched Tg-SwDI cells from 3-month-old mice.
source: When we crossed the Tg-SwDI mouse with a Cdkn2a knockout mouse (Tg-SwDI/Cdkn2a-/-) and performed limiting dilution assays in SVZ cells from 3-month-old mice, there was a complete restoration of the NIC frequency in the Tg-SwDI/Cdkn2a-/- cells compared to age-matched Tg-SwDI cells (p=7.7e–05; Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by limiting dilution assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: NIC rescue was also observed in hippocampal cells cultured from microdissection of the DG in Tg-SwDI/Cdkn2a-/- mice.
source: This NIC rescue was also observed in hippocampal cells cultured from microdissection of the DG (p=2.09e–9, Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by limiting dilution assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Impairment of NPC regeneration is a function of aging that is accelerated by APP mutations and is mitigated through loss of Cdkn2a.
source: These results demonstrate that impairment of NPC regeneration, as measured by NIC frequencies, is a function of aging that is accelerated by APP mutations and is mitigated through loss of Cdkn2a, a known regulator of NPC self-renewal (Molofsky et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and citation to Molofsky et al., 2003.

claim: Mutations or loss of function in the Cdkn2a gene eventually leads to tumor formation.
source: Unfortunately, mutations or loss of function in the Cdkn2a gene eventually leads to tumor formation, making it not feasible to perform limiting dilution experiments in 1-year-old Cdk2na knockout mice and also making it less than ideal to target therapeutically (Hussussian et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hussussian et al., 1994.

claim: USP16 is an antagonist of BMI1 and a de-repressor of Cdkn2a that acts through the enzymatic removal of ubiquitin from histone H2A.
source: Upstream of Cdkn2a is USP16, an antagonist of BMI1 and a de-repressor of Cdkn2a that acts through the enzymatic removal of ubiquitin from histone H2A (Figure 4C; Adorno et al., 2013; Joo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Adorno et al., 2013; Joo et al., 2007 and illustrated in Figure 4C.

claim: Overexpression of USP16 in human-derived neurospheres led to a marked decrease in the formation of secondary neurospheres.
source: This is supported by previous data that showed overexpression of USP16 in human-derived neurospheres led to a marked decrease in the formation of secondary neurospheres (Adorno et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Adorno et al., 2013.

claim: Overexpression of Bmi1 led to increased self-renewal and maintenance of multipotency.
source: and overexpression of Bmi1 led to increased self-renewal and maintenance of multipotency (Fasano et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fasano et al., 2009.

claim: Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice do not show tumor formation.
source: To test this, we crossed Tg-SwDI mice with Usp16+/- mice to generate Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice, which do not show tumor formation.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: Tg-SwDI mice express greater than twofold more cortical Cdkn2a than both WT and Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice.
source: We found that Tg-SwDI mice express greater than twofold more cortical Cdkn2a than both WT and Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice, for which expression levels were very similar (p=0.0365 and p=0.0318, respectively, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice had significantly greater NIC frequencies in the SVZ and DG, partially rescuing the self-renewal defect seen with mutant APP.
source: Limiting dilution experiments of cells isolated from the SVZ and DG of the hippocampus showed that Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice had significantly greater NIC frequencies, partially rescuing the self-renewal defect seen with mutant APP (p=0.0492 and p=0.00233, respectively; Figure 4E, Figure 4—source data 3 and Figure 4F, Figure 4—source data 4).
evidence: This is supported by limiting dilution assay data shown in Figure 4E and 4F.

claim: Two-year-old Tg-SwDI mice show reduced Bmi1 expression, which was rescued by Usp16 haploinsufficiency, in both the SVZ and cortex.
source: Furthermore, two-year-old Tg-SwDI mice show reduced Bmi1 expression, which was rescued by Usp16 haploinsufficiency, in both the SVZ and cortex (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, Reinitz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Reversal of impaired self-renewal in the Tg-SwDI model is possible through targeting Cdkn2a upstream regulator, USP16.
source: Similar to the NIC rescue in the Tg-SwDI/Cdkn2a-/- mice, these data provide further evidence of cell-intrinsic impaired self-renewal in the Tg-SwDI model of familial AD, and that reversal of this impairment is possible through targeting Cdkn2a upstream regulator, USP16.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing rescue of NIC frequencies.

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq was performed on lineage depleted primary FACS-sorted CD31-CD45-TER119-CD24- SVZ cells from Tg-SwDI, WT, and Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice at 3 and 4 months and 1 year of age.
source: To delineate potential self-renewal pathways that might contribute to the defect and rescue of Tg-SwDI NPCs and Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- NPCs, respectively, we performed single-cell RNA-seq on lineage depleted primary FACS-sorted CD31-CD45-TER119-CD24- SVZ cells from Tg-SwDI, WT, and Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice at 3 and 4 months and 1 year of age (Figure 5A; Mootha et al., 2003; Subramanian et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: A cell-type analysis using a TSNE plot did not find any new cell populations specific to the Tg-SwDI genotype.
source: A cell-type analysis using a TSNE plot surveying the top differentially expressed genes of each cluster (Tabula Muris Consortium et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2014) did not find any new cell populations specific to the Tg-SwDI genotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B, Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by TSNE plot analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Changes in phenotype in Tg-SwDI cells are the result of transcriptional differences in cells rather than the addition or subtraction of an existing cell type.
source: This suggested to us that changes in phenotype were the result of transcriptional differences in cells rather than the addition or subtraction of an existing cell type.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TSNE plot analysis.

claim: Cells from the Tg-SwDI mouse model expressed approximately a 1.5-fold increase in both normalized mutant APP expression and endogenous App expression compared to WT cells.
source: Like our human model, cells from the Tg-SwDI mouse model expressed approximately a 1.5-fold increase in both normalized mutant APP expression and endogenous App expression compared to WT cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2—source data 1, Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: No significant transcriptional upregulation of an inflammatory signature was observed in either 3 and 4-month-old or 1-year-old mice between Tg-SwDI and WT mice in single-cell RNA-seq data.
source: In addition, similar to the Luminex screen, we did not observe any significant transcriptional upregulation of an inflammatory signature in either 3 and 4-month-old or 1-year-old mice between Tg-SwDI and WT mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2—source data 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2—source data 3, Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: Only a few genes were significantly different between WT and Tg-SwDI cells at 3 and 4 months or 1 year of age in a panel of proliferation-related genes.
source: Furthermore, when we looked at a panel of proliferation-related genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, B, Figure 5—figure supplement 3—source data 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3—source data 2, Chen et al., 2022), there were only a few genes significantly different between WT and Tg-SwDI cells at 3 and 4 months or 1 year of age
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: The hyperproliferation phenotype observed in 3 and 4-month-old mice might involve upregulation of only a few genes such as Anapc2, Cdk4, and Pcna and downregulation of cell cycle inhibitors Cdkn1a and Cdkn1b.
source: suggesting that the hyperproliferation phenotype we observed in 3 and 4-month-old mice might involve upregulation of only a few genes such as Anapc2, Cdk4, and Pcna and downregulation of cell cycle inhibitors Cdkn1a and Cdkn1b.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq analysis of proliferation-related genes.

claim: Only three gene sets were enriched in Tg-SwDI mice over WT mice and were also rescued in the Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice at both ages: TGF-ß pathway, oxidative phosphorylation, and Myc Targets.
source: Using the GSEA Hallmark gene sets, we found only three gene sets that were enriched in Tg-SwDI mice over WT mice and were also rescued in the Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice at both ages: TGF-ß pathway, oxidative phosphorylation, and Myc Targets (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: The TGF-ß pathway consistently had the highest normalized enrichment score in pairwise comparisons between Tg-SwDI versus WT and Tg-SwDI versus Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- of the three rescued pathways.
source: The TGF-ß pathway consistently had the highest normalized enrichment score in pairwise comparisons between Tg-SwDI versus WT and Tg-SwDI versus Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- of the three rescued pathways (Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5—source data 2.

claim: The leading-edge genes contributing to the enrichment plots of the TGF-ß pathway showed upregulation of BMP receptors and Id genes, which are known to be involved in BMP signaling.
source: In looking specifically at the leading-edge genes contributing to the enrichment plots of the TGF-ß pathway, we found upregulation of BMP receptors and Id genes, which are known to be involved in BMP signaling, a sub-pathway of TGF-ß (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA enrichment plots shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Genes such as Bmpr2, Bmpr1a, Id2, and Id3 were upregulated in Tg-SwDI mice and rescued in Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice.
source: Heatmaps of average normalized single-cell gene expression showed BMP receptors as the most highly expressed TGF-ß receptors, with genes such as Bmpr2, Bmpr1a, Id2, and Id3 upregulated in Tg-SwDI mice and rescued in Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The BMP response Id genes showed stronger localization to the SLC1A3+ NPC clusters of both 3 and 4-month-old and 1-year-old mice than genes of the oxidative phosphorylation and Myc target pathways.
source: Furthermore, the BMP response Id genes showed stronger localization to the SLC1A3+ NPC clusters of both 3 and 4-month-old and 1-year-old mice than genes of the oxidative phosphorylation and Myc target pathways (Figure 5—figure supplements 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by TSNE plots shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 5 and 6.

claim: USP16 may regulate NPC function in part through the BMP pathway.
source: These data suggest that USP16 may regulate NPC function in part through the BMP pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq data showing enrichment and rescue of BMP pathway genes.

claim: Levels of phosphorylated-SMAD (pSMAD) 1, 5, and 8 were significantly increased in mutant APP neurospheres compared to control.
source: First, we measured levels of phosphorylated-SMAD (pSMAD) 1, 5, and 8, known downstream regulators of BMP activity, and found they were significantly increased in the mutant neurospheres compared to control (p=0.0001, Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Treatment of neurospheres with the BMP receptor inhibitor LDN-193189 substantially decreased pSMAD 1/5/8 in APP SwI NPCs.
source: Treatment of the neurospheres with the BMP receptor inhibitor LDN-193189, a specific inhibitor of BMP-mediated SMAD1, SMAD5, and SMAD8 activation, substantially decreased pSMAD 1/5/8 in APP SwI NPCs (p<0.0001, Figure 6B C; Yu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Treatment of neurospheres expressing mutant APP with LDN-193189 for a week resulted in the number of colonies originating from those cells being similar to control cells and significantly higher than untreated mutant APP neurospheres.
source: Furthermore, when we treated neurospheres expressing mutant APP with LDN-193189 for a week, the number of colonies originating from those cells were similar to control cells and significantly higher than untreated mutant APP neurospheres (Figure 6D E).
evidence: This is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 6D and 6E.

claim: LDN-193189 had minimal impact on Zsgreen control neurosphere growth.
source: Notably, LDN-193189 had minimal impact on Zsgreen control neurosphere growth (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The decrease in NIC frequency observed with mutant APP could be explained in part by the upregulation of BMP signaling.
source: This finding demonstrates that the decrease in NIC frequency observed with mutant APP could be explained in part by the upregulation of BMP signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue of colony formation by BMP inhibition.

claim: BMPR inhibition rescues the NPC defect in cells overexpressing mutant APP at doses that have minimal toxicity on healthy cells.
source: Moreover, BMPR inhibition rescues this defect in cells overexpressing mutant APP at doses that have minimal toxicity on healthy cells.
evidence: This is supported by the colony formation assay data showing differential effects on mutant APP versus control cells.

claim: BMP signaling enrichment is recapitulated in human NPCs expressing mutant APP.
source: Altogether, these data reveal that BMP signaling enrichment is recapitulated in human NPCs expressing mutant APP, and that BMPR inhibition normalizes the stem cell defect.
evidence: This is supported by the pSMAD and colony formation data in human neurospheres.

claim: BMPR inhibition normalizes the stem cell defect in human NPCs expressing mutant APP.
source: Altogether, these data reveal that BMP signaling enrichment is recapitulated in human NPCs expressing mutant APP, and that BMPR inhibition normalizes the stem cell defect.
evidence: This is supported by the colony formation assay data showing rescue by LDN-193189.

claim: Increased numbers of GFAP+ astrocytes were seen throughout the cortex of 9–12-month-old Tg-SwDI mice, which were significantly reduced with Usp16 haploinsufficiency.
source: Increased numbers of GFAP+ astrocytes were seen throughout the cortex of 9–12-month-old Tg-SwDI mice, which could mark the beginning of astrogliosis, and were significantly reduced with Usp16 haploinsufficiency (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, see also Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: No difference in plaque burden was observed between 10-month-old Tg-SwDI and age-matched Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice.
source: However, no difference was observed in plaque burden, demonstrated by Thioflavin S staining, in the age-matched Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Thioflavin S staining data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A Luminex screen of 1-year-old Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice did not reveal significant differences in the levels of inflammatory cytokines from any of the groups.
source: In addition, a Luminex screen of 1-year-old Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice also did not reveal significant differences in the levels of inflammatory cytokines from any of the groups (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by Luminex assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: The Tg-SwDI cohort exhibited impaired performance in the NOR task as early as 6 months of age, with preference indexes (PIs) that were not significantly different 24 hr after training.
source: As expected, when studying the cognitive decline in the Tg-SwDI cohort, we found that the Tg-SwDI cohort exhibited impaired performance in the NOR task as early as 6 months of age, with preference indexes (PIs) that were not significantly different 24 hr after training, indicating no memory of the familiar object (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral testing data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice performed equally to their age-matched WT controls in the NOR task, indicating memory of the familiar object with PIs in the 65–70% range.
source: The Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice performed equally to their age-matched WT controls indicating memory of the familiar object with PIs in the 65–70% range (p=0.001 and p=0.0099, respectively; Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral testing data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Long-term memory impairment in Tg-SwDI mice and rescue in Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice was further supported by the Barnes maze where Tg-SwDI mice spent more time exploring off-target quadrants and Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice spent more time in the target quadrant.
source: Long-term memory impairment in Tg-SwDI mice and rescue in Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice was further supported by the Barnes maze (BM) where Tg-SwDI mice spent more time exploring off-target quadrants and Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice spent more time in the target quadrant (p=0.0128 and p=0.0251, respectively; Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by Barnes maze data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Modulating Usp16 gene dosage does not affect amyloid plaque burden but ameliorates stem cell self-renewal defects and some of the cognitive defects in Tg-SwDI mice.
source: These data indicate that although modulating Usp16 gene dosage does not affect amyloid plaque burden, it ameliorates stem cell self-renewal defects that may be the earliest indication of pathology, as well as some of the cognitive defects in these mice that occur later (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data from plaque staining, NIC assays, and behavioral tests.

claim: The lack of robust efficacy in trials that utilize therapies directed against amyloid and inflammatory pathways suggests that other mechanisms are at play in Alzheimer's disease.
source: The lack of robust efficacy in trials that utilize therapies directed against amyloid and inflammatory pathways, even when initiated relatively early in the disease (Selkoe, 2019; Imbimbo et al., 2010), suggests that other mechanisms are at play.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Selkoe, 2019; Imbimbo et al., 2010.

claim: An NPC defect predates the development of measurable inflammation and amyloid plaque accumulation in a mutant APP model.
source: One of the primary findings in this study is that an NPC defect predates the development of measurable inflammation and amyloid plaque accumulation in a mutant APP model and that this defect is cell intrinsic.
evidence: This is supported by the temporal analyses of NPC function, inflammation, and plaque deposition in the study.

claim: The cell intrinsic NPC defect is reproduced in human fetal NPCs expressing APP Swedish and Indiana mutations.
source: We further show this cell intrinsic NPC defect is reproduced in human fetal NPCs expressing APP Swedish and Indiana mutations, suggesting that our findings are translatable to other APP mutations and to human cells.
evidence: This is supported by the limiting dilution assay data in human neurospheres.

claim: The NPC defect discovered in the study is partly regulated by Cdkn2a.
source: The NPC defect that we discovered is partly regulated by Cdkn2a, a central component of aging responsible for decreased neurogenesis and differentiation of NPCs (Abdouh et al., 2012; Molofsky et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the rescue of NPC defects in Tg-SwDI/Cdkn2a-/- mice and citations to Abdouh et al., 2012; Molofsky et al., 2006.

claim: CDKN2A expression has been correlated with sporadic AD.
source: Because CDKN2A expression has been correlated with sporadic AD (Arendt et al., 1996; Lüth et al., 2000; McShea et al., 1997)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arendt et al., 1996; Lüth et al., 2000; McShea et al., 1997.

claim: Targeting CDKN2A has shown benefit in improving age related and sporadic AD in models.
source: and targeting CDKN2A has shown benefit in improving age related and sporadic AD in models, we speculate our findings may have relevance for treatment of sporadic AD.
evidence: This is speculation based on previous studies and the findings of this study.

claim: Removal of p16Ink4a-positive senescent cells has been shown to attenuate progression of age-related decline and preserve cognitive function in both an accelerated aging AD mouse model and a tauopathy mouse model.
source: Removal of the p16Ink4a-positive senescent cells, for instance, using a suicide gene under the regulation of the Cdkn2a promoter has been shown to attenuate progression of age-related decline and preserve cognitive function in both an accelerated aging AD mouse model and a tauopathy mouse model (Baker et al., 2011; Bussian et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baker et al., 2011; Bussian et al., 2018.

claim: The use of a suicide gene is not directly translatable into humans.
source: However, the use of a suicide gene is not directly translatable into humans
evidence: This is a statement of practical limitation.

claim: Other senolytics such as BCL2-inhibitors or the combination of Dasatinib and quercetin have toxicities which can limit their use.
source: and other senolytics such as BCL2-inhibitors or the combination of Dasatinib and quercetin have toxicities which can limit their use (Amaya-Montoya et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Amaya-Montoya et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2015.

claim: USP16 is proposed as a novel target that might circumvent many of the problems associated with CDKN2A inhibition or with senolytics' treatment.
source: Here, we propose USP16 as a novel target that might circumvent many of the problems associated with CDKN2A inhibition or with senolytics' treatment.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the findings of the study.

claim: Inhibiting USP16 by making Tg-SwDI mice haploinsufficient for Usp16 resulted in a rescue in the self-renewal of NPCs as early as 3 months of age.
source: When we inhibited USP16 by making Tg-SwDI mice haploinsufficient for Usp16 (Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/-), we found a rescue in the self-renewal of NPCs as early as 3 months of age.
evidence: This is supported by limiting dilution assay data in Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice.

claim: A new role for USP16 in regulating the BMP pathway was demonstrated, a mechanism independent of Cdkn2a.
source: We also demonstrated a new role for USP16 in regulating the BMP pathway, a mechanism independent of Cdkn2a.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data showing enrichment and rescue of BMP pathway genes.

claim: Bmi1 represses BMP signaling.
source: Previously, Gargiulo et al. found that self-renewal gene Bmi1, whose PRC1 activity is counterbalanced by USP16, represses BMP signaling (Gargiulo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gargiulo et al., 2013.

claim: NPCs from Bmi1 knockout mice treated with BMP4 experience even further growth arrest than those untreated.
source: NPCs from Bmi1 knockout mice treated with BMP4 experience even further growth arrest than those untreated (Gargiulo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gargiulo et al., 2013.

claim: Treatment of human neural stem cells with secreted APPα or overexpression of APP promoted phosphorylation of SMAD 1/5/8 and induced massive glial differentiation through the BMP pathway.
source: Furthermore, Kwak, Lohuizen, and colleagues showed that treatment of human neural stem cells with secreted APPα or overexpression of APP promoted phosphorylation of SMAD 1/5/8 and induced massive glial differentiation (by expression of GFAP) through the BMP pathway (Kwak et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kwak et al., 2014.

claim: Expression of mutant APP in human fetal NPCs induced phosphorylation of SMAD 1/5/8 and reduced neurosphere colony formation that was rescued by a BMP receptor inhibitor.
source: In line with this, our results reveal expression of mutant APP in human fetal NPCs induced phosphorylation of SMAD 1/5/8 and reduced neurosphere colony formation that was rescued by a BMP receptor inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by the pSMAD and colony formation data in human neurospheres.

claim: The findings of astrogliosis extend to an in vivo mouse model of AD.
source: Importantly, our data extends their findings of astrogliosis to an in vivo mouse model of AD.
evidence: This is supported by the GFAP staining data in Tg-SwDI mice.

claim: BMI1 regulates both Cdkn2a and the BMP pathway independently.
source: Interestingly, BMI1 regulates both Cdkn2a and the BMP pathway independently
evidence: This is an inference based on the literature and the findings of the study.

claim: BMI1 expression was shown to be decreased in AD patients compared to age-matched controls.
source: and BMI1 expression was shown to be decreased in AD patients compared to age-matched controls (Flamier et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Flamier et al., 2018.

claim: The timing of therapeutic treatment in AD seems to be crucial as studies have shown that treating the disease too late has little efficacy.
source: The timing of therapeutic treatment in AD seems to be crucial as studies have shown that treating the disease too late has little efficacy (Sperling et al., 2011; Yiannopoulou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sperling et al., 2011; Yiannopoulou et al., 2019.

claim: The Tg-SwDI mice develop cognitive defects after the accumulation of amyloid beta plaques, a timeline which mimics that of humans with both dominantly inherited AD and late-onset sporadic AD.
source: The Tg-SwDI mice used in our study develop cognitive defects after the accumulation of amyloid beta plaques, a timeline which mimics that of humans with both dominantly inherited AD and late-onset sporadic AD (Bateman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bateman et al., 2012.

claim: 31% of healthy control subjects had high PiB retention indicating Aß deposition and of these, 25% developed mild cognitive impairment or AD by 3 years.
source: In a study characterizing sporadic AD, for instance, Villemagne et al. used Pittsburgh compound B (PiB) positron emission tomography (PET) to show that 31% of healthy control subjects had high PiB retention indicating Aß deposition and of these, 25% developed mild cognitive impairment or AD by 3 years (Villemagne et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Villemagne et al., 2011.

claim: Treating the plaques alone did not rescue cognitive defects in studies by Salloway et al. and Biogen's EMERGE and ENGAGE trials.
source: Furthermore, studies such as those by Salloway et al. and Biogen's EMERGE and ENGAGE trials found that treating the plaques alone did not rescue cognitive defects (Knopman et al., 2021; Salloway et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Knopman et al., 2021; Salloway et al., 2014.

claim: Amyloid-ß oligomers may impair neurogenesis and promote gliogenesis of human NPCs through the GSK-3ß pathway.
source: Although the mechanism for how mutant APP causes an NPC defect is outside the scope of this work, it has been postulated that amyloid-ß oligomers may impair neurogenesis and promote gliogenesis of human NPCs through the GSK-3ß pathway which unfortunately is not amenable to inhibition as it phosphorylates a variety of substrates and incurs large cytotoxic off-target effects (Bernabeu-Zornoza et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bernabeu-Zornoza et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2013.

claim: Early therapeutic reduction of USP16 or BMP signaling in neural stem cells may reverse the neurogenic defect that may contribute to symptomatic AD later in life, especially if applied before cognitive deficits are present in the patient.
source: The translatability of our study therefore comes from observing that early therapeutic reduction of USP16 or BMP signaling in neural stem cells may reverse the neurogenic defect that may contribute to symptomatic AD later in life, especially if applied before cognitive deficits are present in the patient.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: USP16 reduction reduced astrocyte proliferation and restored cognitive function as measured by the NOR and Barnes Maze tests, independently of plaques and widespread inflammation.
source: It is important to note that USP16 reduction also reduced astrocyte proliferation and restored cognitive function as measured by the NOR and Barnes Maze tests, independently of plaques and widespread inflammation.
evidence: This is supported by the GFAP staining and behavioral testing data in Tg-SwDI/Usp16+/- mice.

claim: The increase in GFAP-expressing cells and impaired cognitive function seen in the Tg-SwDI model are purely attributable to mutant APP as Tg-SwDI mice do not develop neurofibrillary tangles that require mutations in tau.
source: The increase in GFAP-expressing cells and impaired cognitive function seen in this AD model are purely attributable to mutant APP as Tg-SwDI mice do not develop neurofibrillary tangles that require mutations in tau (Wilcock et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wilcock et al., 2008 and the characteristics of the Tg-SwDI model.

claim: Therapeutic strategies that combine targeting USP16 with agents that target extracellular plaque formation, neurofibrillary tangles, and/or inflammation may improve treatments for AD.
source: Thus, therapeutic strategies that combine targeting USP16, which effectively rescue the mutant APP-induced cell intrinsic damage, with agents that target extracellular plaque formation, neurofibrillary tangles, and/or inflammation may improve treatments for AD.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings of the study.
